Tencent and battery maker CATL are among the biggest backers.
It comes two days after a US order told federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek products.

paragraphs.text: DeepSeek, the Hangzhou-based developer of the R1 reasoning model, is wrapping up a funding round that has raised about 100 billion yuan, or roughly $14.98 billion, from existing and new investors, Reuters reported on October 22, 2026, citing people with knowledge of the matter. Bloomberg first reported the $15 billion figure.

According to Reuters, the total is double the 50 billion yuan the company originally set out to raise. The round is expected to close in the coming days, and one source told Reuters the financial terms were not final and could still change. DeepSeek, CATL and Tencent could not be reached for comment, Reuters said, and DeepSeek did not immediately respond to TechCrunch.

Battery maker Contemporary Amperex Technology, known as CATL, and Tencent, the operator of WeChat, are among the largest investors, according to Reuters and Bloomberg. Reuters noted that many of the backers are supported by the state or by large corporations. Tech Startups, citing Reuters, listed more than 15 investors, including Geely, Meituan, Midea, NetEase and IDG Capital, and put the pre-money valuation at about 500 billion yuan, or $74 billion.

The round would be far larger than DeepSeek's earlier fundraising. TechCrunch reported that the company raised more than $7 billion at a $50 billion valuation in June and was reported in July to be seeking another $1.5 billion at about $71 billion. DeepSeek was founded in 2023 by Liang Wenfeng, a co-founder of the quantitative hedge fund High-Flyer, who holds an estimated 81.6% stake in the Chinese operating entity according to an analysis by WireScreen cited by TechCrunch.

The funding news arrived two days after the Department of Homeland Security published an order in the Federal Register on October 20 directing federal civilian agencies to stop buying DeepSeek products and to remove them from government IT systems. The order also covers third-party products and services built with DeepSeek technology, and agencies may request exceptions.

The Hacker News reported that the order was signed on July 24, 2026, under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018, and was filed for public inspection on October 19. BleepingComputer reported that agencies have 60 days to submit exception requests, which the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency will review, and that the order is not a general ban on private or consumer use.

DHS cited concerns that Chinese authorities could potentially access sensitive information from US government users under Chinese law, according to TechCrunch. China's foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Beijing opposes overstretching the concept of national security and politicizing technology and trade issues.

Several parts of the US government had already restricted DeepSeek. The Hacker News reported that Congress, NASA, the Navy, the Pentagon and the state of Texas had barred it from government devices by February 2025.

Reuters reported in September that DeepSeek hired CITIC Securities to prepare for a potential listing on Shanghai's STAR Market, and said the new round signals the company is moving closer to public markets. In September, DeepSeek also released DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, which the company said offers faster inference and higher throughput.

The timing shows how little the federal procurement order touches DeepSeek's core business. The order limits what US civilian agencies can install, while the company's new money comes almost entirely from large Chinese corporations and state-linked investors, many of them suppliers in China's own technology chain.

The next markers are the formal close of the round, the final valuation, and whether DeepSeek files for the STAR Market listing it has been preparing, along with any exception requests US agencies submit within the 60-day window.
